questions.q: What problem does 'automation sprawl' create on an object like Case?
options: It makes the object's page layout load faster
Unpredictable execution order, harder debugging, and the risk of flows silently conflicting with each other
It automatically bulkifies all the flows
It prevents any flow from being activated
questions.explain: Many independently built flows on the same object/trigger make order hard to predict, debugging harder, and create risk of conflicting updates.

questions.q: What is Salesforce's official recommendation for record-triggered flows on a given object?
options: Build as many flows as needed, one per business rule
Always use Process Builder instead of Flow for new automation
Never trigger more than one flow per org
One flow per object per trigger context, using Decision elements to branch between the different pieces of logic
questions.explain: Salesforce recommends consolidating logic into one flow per object per trigger context (e.g., one Before-Save flow), with Decision elements routing to the right logic.

questions.q: In the lesson's five-flow example, what changes when the logic is consolidated into one flow?
options: The business rules themselves change to be simpler
Four of the five rules are deleted entirely
The business rules stay the same — only where that logic lives changes, now as Decision branches in one flow
The rules are moved into Apex triggers instead
questions.explain: Consolidation doesn't change what the automation does — it changes where the logic lives, making it one place to read and debug instead of five.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should you build a brand-new flow instead of extending an existing one?
options: Every time, regardless of what already exists
Only on weekends, per a Salesforce scheduling rule
Never — all automation for an org must live in a single flow
Only when there's genuinely no existing flow for that object and trigger context
questions.explain: The standing discipline is to check for an existing flow on that object/trigger context first, and extend it with a Decision branch rather than add another flow.

questions.q: Why is relying on Salesforce's flow execution order across many independently built flows considered fragile?
options: Because every new flow added to the object changes the picture, and nobody reliably reviews the full list before adding one more
Because execution order is purely random and documented nowhere
Because Salesforce deprecated execution order settings
Because flows cannot be ordered at all, only Apex triggers can
questions.explain: Even though Salesforce does define an order, depending on it across many scattered flows is fragile since each new addition changes the full picture.
